--- title: Sklearn workflow aliases: - /ai/sk_workflow.html author: - Marie-Hélène Burle - Modified from [Matthew Greenberg](https://profiles.ucalgary.ca/matthew-greenberg) (UCalgary) for [M2PI](https://m2pi.ca/) --- :::{.def} Scikit-learn has a very clean and consistent API, making it very easy to use: a similar workflow can be applied to most techniques. Let's go over two examples. ::: ## Load packages ::: {#a4ed55f1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.datasets import fetch_california_housing, load_breast_cancer from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, LogisticRegression from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier from sklearn.metrics import ( mean_squared_error, mean_absolute_percentage_error, accuracy_score ) import polars as pl import matplotlib from matplotlib import pyplot as plt import numpy as np from collections import Counter ``` ::: ## Example 1: California housing ### Load and explore the data ::: {#b322940d .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} cal_housing = fetch_california_housing() type(cal_housing) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` sklearn.utils._bunch.Bunch ``` ::: ::: Let's look at the attributes of `cal_housing`: ::: {#69166a74 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} dir(cal_housing) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['DESCR', 'data', 'feature_names', 'frame', 'target', 'target_names'] ``` ::: ::: ::: {#a2c11921 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} cal_housing.feature_names ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` ['MedInc', 'HouseAge', 'AveRooms', 'AveBedrms', 'Population', 'AveOccup', 'Latitude', 'Longitude'] ``` ::: ::: ::: {#935530bf .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(cal_housing.DESCR) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` .. _california_housing_dataset: California Housing dataset -------------------------- **Data Set Characteristics:** :Number of Instances: 20640 :Number of Attributes: 8 numeric, predictive attributes and the target :Attribute Information: - MedInc median income in block group - HouseAge median house age in block group - AveRooms average number of rooms per household - AveBedrms average number of bedrooms per household - Population block group population - AveOccup average number of household members - Latitude block group latitude - Longitude block group longitude :Missing Attribute Values: None This dataset was obtained from the StatLib: https://lib.stat.cmu.edu/datasets/houses.zip The target variable is the median house value for California districts, expressed in hundreds of thousands of dollars ($100,000). This dataset was derived from the 1990 U.S. census, using one row per census block group. A block group is the smallest geographical unit for which the U.S. Census Bureau publishes sample data (a block group typically has a population of 600 to 3,000 people). A household is a group of people residing within a home. Since the average number of rooms and bedrooms in this dataset are provided per household, these columns may take surprisingly large values for block groups with few households and many empty houses, such as vacation resorts. It can be downloaded/loaded using the :func:`sklearn.datasets.fetch_california_housing` function. .. rubric:: References - Pace, R. Kelley and Ronald Barry, Sparse Spatial Autoregressions, Statistics and Probability Letters, 33:291-297, 1997. ``` ::: ::: ::: {#23f78347 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} X = cal_housing.data y = cal_housing.target ``` ::: :::{.note} This can also be obtained with `X, y = fetch_california_housing(return_X_y=True)`. ::: Let's have a look at the shape of `X` and `y`: ::: {#dc3ff427 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} X.shape ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` (20640, 8) ``` ::: ::: ::: {#8e613043 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} y.shape ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` (20640,) ``` ::: ::: While not at all necessary, we can turn this bunch object into a more familiar data frame to explore the data further: ::: {#5a62f5a8 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} cal_housing_df = pl.DataFrame(cal_housing.data, schema=cal_housing.feature_names) ``` ::: ::: {#2d7edc30 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} cal_housing_df.head() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}
